notes: The last clause is difficult. It can mean that enslavement would not warrant troubling the king, or that the enemy could not compensate for the king’s loss. Esther’s argument distinguishes enslavement from the planned destruction.
The king accuses Haman of assaulting Esther. The narrator has described Haman falling onto her couch while pleading for his life.
The Hebrew names a wooden structure fifty cubits high. Whether execution involved hanging or impalement is uncertain. “Stake” continues the wording of chapter 5.
vocabulary: Esther uses the language of sale for the people’s delivery into the enemy’s power.
An ancient measure based on the forearm; fifty cubits was roughly seventy-five feet.

notes: The Hebrew terms for the couriers’ horses are uncommon. The wording identifies swift animals of royal breeding without treating every term as a separate species.

The decree permits lethal action and plunder. Its mention of children and women can attach to the hostile population being destroyed or to the Jews being attacked. The draft keeps the former reading; the ambiguity should not be used to hide the decree’s disturbing breadth.
The rare verb can mean becoming Jews or identifying themselves as Jews. The text gives fear of the Jews as the motive; it does not describe an inward conversion.
vocabulary: The royal seal authenticated a decree issued in the king’s name.
The decree authorizes retaliation; its language goes beyond simply escaping danger.

notes: The refusal to take plunder recurs in verses 15 and 16, although the second decree had permitted it.
Haman’s sons have already been killed in verses 7–10. Esther now requests the public display of their bodies on the wooden structure.
“When the matter came” may also be read “when she came,” referring to Esther. This summary compresses events recounted at greater length earlier.
“Peace and assurance” renders an expression literally linking peace and truth or reliability.
vocabulary: The plural of pur, the lot cast to choose the date for the Jews’ destruction.
The commemoration includes sharing food with one another and giving to those in need.

notes: “The many among his brothers” does not explicitly say everyone. The final phrase, literally “all his offspring,” can refer more broadly to his people or to their descendants.
vocabulary: Payment exacted by an imperial ruler from subject territories.
